title: Who You Call
hook: You saw it. Now you have to say it.
scene: Rain still, same viaduct, you already gave the gap. The two cars are behind you now. Radios are trash and monitored. A witness still has a number to call when someone is hurt or the road is blocked. You pull onto a legal pad at the next ramp. The tablet can dial. What you say is where, how many cars, whether anyone is moving, whether the lanes are dead. Not a story. Not a guess about fault.
decision: You are on a pad and you saw the crash. What do you do now?

options.text: Keep rolling — you already looked, and radios are trash anyway
options.result: You leave a blocked viaduct with no sentence on it. The next car gets no warning. Looking is not reporting. The pad you skipped was the call.

options.text: Call and tell them it was the gray car's fault because you saw it first
options.result: You get someone on the line and spend it on a verdict. They still do not have a mile marker or a count. Fault is a later job. You burned the call on a guess.

options.text: Post it to the convoy board so someone closer can deal with it
options.result: The board just passes talk. Nobody has a location they can send. You handed a crash to a chorus. The viaduct stays a rumor.

options.text: Call 911. Where you are, two cars, lanes blocked, you did not see anyone moving
options.result: You give the ramp, the viaduct, two cars, doors open, no one standing that you saw. They repeat it back. You stay on the pad until they release you. That is a report, not a story.

debrief: If you witness a crash, pull off and call 911. Say where, how many vehicles, whether people are moving, whether lanes are blocked. The ramp pad holds the call.

source.psdp_skill: Skill ten: city driving – part two
source.teaching_target: Report a witnessed crash by calling 911; give location, vehicle count, injuries if known, and whether the roadway is blocked — not fault.
